named.name: Preparation of alkyl halide from alcohol using thionyl chloride
named.tip: Best lab method because SO2 and HCl escape as gases, leaving pure alkyl chloride; examiners ask 'why is this the best method'.

named.name: Finkelstein reaction
named.tip: NaBr/NaCl formed is insoluble in dry acetone, driving equilibrium forward; a common fill-in-the-blank question.

named.name: Swarts reaction
named.cond: AgF or Hg2F2 or CoF2 or SbF3
named.tip: Used specifically to prepare alkyl fluorides; students often confuse it with Finkelstein (iodide) reaction.

named.name: Wurtz reaction
named.tip: Gives symmetrical alkane with double the carbon atoms; fails to give good yield for unsymmetrical products, mention 'dry ether' condition.

named.name: Wurtz-Fittig reaction
named.tip: Used to attach an alkyl group to benzene ring; distinguish from Fittig reaction (only aryl halides, gives biphenyl type product).

named.name: Fittig reaction
named.tip: Only aryl halides used, product is diphenyl (biphenyl); common confusion with Wurtz-Fittig.

named.name: Williamson synthesis (ether formation from haloalkane)
named.tip: Works best with primary alkyl halides; tertiary halides give elimination (alkene) instead due to steric hindrance - frequently tested.

named.name: Dehydrohalogenation (elimination) of alkyl halide
named.tip: Alcoholic KOH gives elimination (alkene) while aqueous KOH gives substitution (alcohol) - a classic exam distinction.

named.name: Nitration of chlorobenzene (electrophilic substitution)
named.tip: Cl is o,p-directing but deactivating due to -I effect dominating over +R effect; explain this duality when asked.

named.name: Hydrolysis of chlorobenzene to phenol (Dow process)
named.tip: Needs high temperature and pressure because aryl halides resist nucleophilic substitution (C-Cl bond strengthened by resonance); common HOTS question.

conversions.q: Convert ethanol to ethyl chloride (HSC style)
steps: step 1: CH3CH2OH + SOCl2 -> CH3CH2Cl + SO2 + HCl (SOCl2, warm)
conversions.ans: Ethanol + SOCl2 gives ethyl chloride directly (best method, pure product).
Wurtz reaction on ethyl bromide gives n-butane.

conversions.q: Convert ethyl bromide to ethyl iodide
steps: step 1: CH3CH2Br + NaI -> CH3CH2I + NaBr (dry acetone, Finkelstein reaction)
conversions.ans: Treat ethyl bromide with NaI in dry acetone (Finkelstein reaction) to get ethyl iodide.

conversions.q: Convert methyl bromide to methyl fluoride
steps: step 1: CH3Br + AgF -> CH3F + AgBr (Swarts reaction)
conversions.ans: Treat methyl bromide with AgF (Swarts reaction) to get methyl fluoride.

steps: step 1: CH3CH2Br + KOH(aq) -> CH3CH2OH + KBr (aqueous KOH, SN2 substitution)
conversions.ans: Aqueous KOH substitutes bromide to give ethanol.

steps: step 1: CH3CH2Br + KOH(alc) -> CH2=CH2 + KBr + H2O (alcoholic KOH, dehydrohalogenation)
conversions.ans: Alcoholic KOH causes elimination of HBr to give ethene.

steps: step 1: C6H5Cl + NaOH -> C6H5OH + NaCl (623 K, 300 atm, Dow process)
conversions.ans: Hydrolyse chlorobenzene with NaOH under high temperature and pressure (Dow process) to get phenol.

conversions.q: Convert bromobenzene and bromoethane to ethylbenzene
steps: step 1: C6H5Br + CH3CH2Br + 2Na -> C6H5CH2CH3 + 2NaBr (dry ether, Wurtz-Fittig reaction)
conversions.ans: Wurtz-Fittig reaction of bromobenzene with ethyl bromide and Na gives ethylbenzene.
